paragraphs.text: On April sixteenth, nineteen ninety-one, Bernie Madoff said he bought one hundred and twenty-three call options on Procter and Gamble stock.
One problem. In the entire market, that whole day, only twenty of those options changed hands.
He claimed six times more than existed. And nobody stopped him for seventeen more years.
By the time it collapsed, the fake balances said sixty-five billion dollars.
Here's the thing. That impossible number isn't a fluke. The biggest frauds in history all hide one. A number that cannot exist.
Today, three of them. A coupon scam from nineteen twenty. A tank farm full of water. And the fund that almost never lost.
And by the end, you'll have a three-question test that would have caught all three. Because the next one won't call itself a Ponzi scheme.
Chapter one. The coupon that couldn't exist.
Boston, nineteen twenty. Banks are paying about five percent a year. And a former dishwasher named Charles Ponzi is promising fifty percent, in forty-five days.
His pitch sounded clever. International reply coupons. Little slips you could buy cheap in Europe, where money was weak after the war, and trade in America for stamps worth more.
Buy low there, cash in high here. On paper, that's arbitrage. It's even legal.
And for a while, it looked like it worked. Early investors got paid, on time. Word spread. By July, money was pouring in at close to a million dollars a day.
Even most of Boston's police force bought in.
But nobody did the math. Until a financial journalist named Clarence Barron did.
To cover what Ponzi owed, a hundred and sixty million postal coupons would have to be in circulation. The actual number? About twenty-seven thousand.
That's not a little short. That's about one coupon for every six thousand he'd need.
So where were the profits coming from? The next investor. Old investors were paid with new investors' money. That's the whole trick.
When the papers ran the numbers, the line outside his office turned into a run. Six banks went down. Investors lost about twenty million dollars. In nineteen twenty.
Ponzi pleaded guilty to mail fraud. His name became the word for the scam. And he died broke, with an estate of seventy-five dollars.
Ponzi's impossible number was hiding in coupons. The next one was hiding in plain sight, inside a tank.
Chapter two. More oil than America.
New Jersey, the early nineteen sixties. Tino De Angelis runs a vegetable oil company called Allied Crude, out of a run-down tank farm in Bayonne.
His business ran on a simple kind of loan. Oil sits in a tank. A warehouse company checks the tank and writes a receipt. Banks lend money against the receipt.
And the company writing those receipts? A unit of American Express. If American Express vouched for the oil, the banks paid.
So De Angelis made more oil. Not real oil. Receipt oil.
Some tanks had hidden compartments, so inspectors saw oil at the hatch. Others were mostly water, because oil floats. Inspectors looked at the top, saw oil, and signed.
And when they walked to the next tank, pipes moved the same oil ahead of them. The same oil, counted again, and again.
Here's the impossible number. By nineteen sixty-three, Allied claimed more soybean and cottonseed oil than existed in the entire United States.
On paper, nine hundred thousand tons. Actually there, about fifty-five thousand. Over ninety percent of it never existed.
Then he tried to corner the market in oil futures. When prices cracked in November nineteen sixty-three, the margin calls came, and somebody finally looked inside the tanks.
Fifty-one lenders. More than a hundred and eighty million dollars in losses. The American Express warehouse unit went bankrupt. A Wall Street brokerage went under.
De Angelis pleaded guilty and was sentenced to twenty years. He was out in seven.
Coupons. Tanks. Both frauds needed more of something than the world actually had. But the biggest one in history needed something even rarer. A perfect record.
Chapter three. The fund that almost never lost.
Bernie Madoff wasn't a nobody. He'd been chairman of the Nasdaq. His trading firm was one of the biggest market makers on Wall Street.
And his investment fund had a pitch that sounded almost boring. No fifty percent. Just steady returns, around ten percent a year. Year after year after year.
That was the genius of it. Ponzi sold greed. Madoff sold safety.
One fund reported ten and a half percent a year for seventeen years. In late two thousand eight, while markets were crashing, it said it was still up for the year.
Now picture a real investment chart. It wiggles. It drops. It has bad months and bad years. Madoff's line went up at an almost perfect forty-five degree angle.
A financial analyst named Harry Markopolos was asked to copy Madoff's strategy. He later said he knew within five minutes that the numbers didn't add up. It took him four hours to prove it.
His red flags were math. Madoff reported losing months only about four percent of the time. Real markets don't move like that.
And the strategy itself was impossible. To make the trades Madoff claimed, he would have needed more options on the Chicago Board Options Exchange than actually existed.
Same pattern as nineteen ninety-one. A hundred and twenty-three options claimed. Twenty traded.
Markopolos took his math to the S E C in two thousand. And again. In two thousand five, he sent a memo titled, The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud.
Over sixteen years, regulators looked at Madoff's firm at least eight times. They didn't find the fraud.
Then two thousand eight happened. Markets crashed, and investors asked for their money back. About seven billion dollars of it.
Madoff's bank account, which had held over five billion dollars earlier that year, was down to about two hundred and thirty-four million.
On December tenth, he told his sons he was finished, and that the fund was a Ponzi scheme. They went to the authorities. The next morning, he was arrested.

Prosecutors put the fraud at sixty-four point eight billion dollars, based on the fake statements. Markopolos estimated that thirty-five to fifty-five billion of that was profit that never existed at all.
Madoff pleaded guilty to eleven federal crimes and was sentenced to a hundred and fifty years. He died in prison in twenty twenty-one.
So here's the impossible number test. Three questions. They would have caught all three.
Question one. Does the math need more of something than exists? More coupons. More oil. More options. If a return needs a market bigger than the market, it's not a return.
Question two. Is it too smooth? Real money wiggles. If something never has a bad month, that's not skill. That's a story.
Question three. Can anyone check it besides them? Ponzi kept his books on index cards. De Angelis's inspectors had close ties to him. Madoff ran his own brokerage, so he checked his own homework.
Three frauds. Three different eras. One pattern. A number that can't exist.
So next time someone shows you a perfect chart, don't ask how much you could make. Ask what it would take for it to be true.
Subscribe for the next case, and tell me in the comments which red flag would have caught you first. Then watch the tank that fooled American Express.
